courses.subject: AIST
courses.title: Numerical Optimization
courses.description: This course aims to provide students with the basic knowledge of optimization theory and introduce various computational libraries and programming techniques to perform optimization. Topics include unconstrained optimization methods, conjugate gradient methods, quasi-newton methods, theory of constrained optimization, linear programming, non-linear constrained optimization, etc.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
Pre-requisite: ENGG1120/ESTR1005 or ENGG1130/ESTR1006 or MATH1510
Not for students who have taken AIST3030 or ESTR3112 or ESTR3114
courses.learning_outcomes:
At the end of the course of studies, students will have acquired the ability to
1. formulate unconstrained optimization problems
2. solve unconstrained optimization problems, either analytically or via computing modules
3. formulate constrained optimization problems
4. solve constrained optimization problems, either analytically or via computing modules
courses.course_syllabus: This course aims to provide students with the basic knowledge of optimization theory and introduce various computational libraries and programming techniques to perform optimization. Topics include unconstrained optimization methods, conjugate gradient methods, quasi-newton methods, theory of constrained optimization, linear programming, non-linear constrained optimization, etc.

courses.subject: AIST
courses.title: Structured Data Modeling and Graph Neural Network
courses.description: This course introduces advanced topics in structured data modeling with a unifying perspective based on graph neural networks (GNNs). Students will study how diverse data types such as images, sequences, and general graphs can be modeled within this framework, covering core architectures including CNNs, RNNs, GNNs, Transformers, and Mamba. The course also explores a broad range of applications in physics, chemistry, materials science, biology, environmental science, as well as pretraining, multi-task learning, multimodal modeling, foundation models, and knowledge graph learning.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Prerequisite: AIST3120 or CSCI3230 or ESTR3108 or CSCI3320
courses.learning_outcomes:
At the end of the course of studies, students will be able to:
1. Demonstrate a solid understanding of the fundamental models and algorithms for graph mining and graph neural networks.
2. Implement and critically evaluate selected graph neural network models and algorithms introduced in the course.
3. Apply the acquired knowledge to design and carry out a project addressing a real-world problem.
4. Communicate clearly and effectively about the application of graph neural networks to practical problem-solving.
courses.course_syllabus:
Week 1. Overview: structured data as graph
Week 2. Spectral graph theory
Week 3. Message passing neural network
Week 4. Sequence as graph
Week 5. Image as graph
Week 6. Applications (1) pretraining and multi-task learning
Week 7. Applications (2) physics, chemistry, and material science
Week 8. Applications (3) biology and environmental science
Week 9. Applications (4) knowledge graph learning
Week 10. Applications (5) multi-modal learning
Week 11. Applications (6) foundation model
Week 12. Presentation (1)
Week 13. Presentation (2)
courses.feedback_evaluation:
1. Quiz and examinations
2. Course evaluation and questionnaire
3. Question-and-answer sessions during class
4. Student consultation during office hours or online

2. Mining Graph Data, Diane J. Cook and Lawrence B. Holder, John Wiley & Sons (2006)
3. Introduction to Graph Neural Networks, Zhiyuan Liu and Jie Zhou, Morgan & Claypool (March 20, 2020)

courses.subject: AIST
courses.title: Embodied Intelligence: Algorithms and Applications
courses.description: Embodied intelligence represents a paradigm where intelligent systems achieve cognition through physical interaction with their environment, with recent breakthroughs enabling transformative applications in autonomous systems. This course aims at providing students with fundamental knowledge and techniques in embodied intelligence, covering theoretical foundations of scene recognition, machine learning methods, multimodal interaction technologies, and policy learning algorithms including reinforcement learning and imitation learning. Application domains such as autonomous navigation, healthcare, and human-robot interaction will be covered. Through lectures, assignments, and project exercises, students will acquire theoretical understanding and practical skills in developing embodied intelligent systems and technologies.
courses.learning_outcomes:
At the end of the course of studies, students will be able to:
1. Design and implement embodied intelligent systems in simulation environments. Develop intelligent agents in physics simulators (PyBullet, Isaac Gym, or MuJoCo) that integrate virtual sensors (RGB cameras, depth sensors) and actuators to interact with simulated environments. Grasp embodied AI interactions with large language models and vision-language models.
2. Apply reinforcement learning and imitation learning for different tasks. Implement and train RL algorithms (DQN, PPO, SAC) and imitation learning methods (behavioral cloning, DAgger) using standard frameworks (Stable-Baselines3, RLlib) to solve navigation, grasping, and manipulation tasks, and understand sim-to-real transfer principles.
3. Process and fuse multimodal sensor data for problem solving. Use computer vision libraries (OpenCV, PyTorch Vision) to process RGB images and depth maps, implement sensor fusion algorithms to combine camera and LiDAR data, and build perception pipelines that enable robots to detect objects, estimate poses, and make decisions in both simulation and real-world applications.
courses.course_syllabus:
Week 1: What is Embodied Intelligence?
Week 2: Camera and Vision Systems
Week 3: LiDAR and 3D Sensing Technologies
Week 4: Multimodal Perception
Week 5: Reinforcement Learning Fundamentals
Week 6: Policy Gradient Methods
Week 7: Imitation Learning
Week 8: VLM-based Planning
Week 9: Embodied AI Applications in Autonomous Driving
Week 10: Embodied AI Applications in Elderly Caring
Week 11: Embodied AI Applications in Healthcare
Week 12: Human-machine Partnership in Embodied AI
Week 13: Future Trends and Ethical Considerations
courses.recommended_readings:
1. Pfeifer, R., & Bongard, J. (2006). How the Body Shapes the Way We Think: A New View of Intelligence. MIT Press.
2. Russell, S., & Norvig, P. (2021). Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (4th Edition). Pearson.
3. Sutton, R. S., & Barto, A. G. (2018). Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd Edition). MIT Press.
4. Goodfellow, I., Bengio, Y., & Courville, A. (2016). Deep Learning. MIT Press.
5. Thrun, S., Burgard, W., & Fox, D. (2005). Probabilistic Robotics. MIT Press.

courses.subject: AIST
courses.title: Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence
courses.description: This course introduces the principles and techniques of Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence (Trustworthy AI), which aims to mitigate the potential adverse effects of AI on people and society. The course focuses on four main aspects of trustworthy AI: privacy & security, robustness, explainability, and fairness. It covers the state-of-the-art research progress in these areas, including federated learning and adversarial attacks. Algorithms, models, and systems will be covered. Moreover, the course discusses the ethical and social implications of trustworthy AI, to foster social awareness among students who would use or develop AI techniques in the future. This course is suitable for students who have some background in machine learning, probability, and linear algebra.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
For students in MSc Computer Science; or
For students in MPhil-PhD Computer Science & Engineering
courses.course_syllabus:
Week 1. Introduction to trustworthy AI
Week 2. Privacy & Security: federated learning basics
Week 3. Privacy & Security: reconstruction attacks and inference attacks
Week 4. Privacy & Security: anonymization, noise injection, SMPC, and homomorphic encryption
Week 5. Robustness: outliers and adversarial attacks
Week 6. Robustness: adversarial detection and defense
Week 7. Explainability: ante-hoc explainability
Week 8. Explainability: post-hoc explainability
Week 9. Fairness: individual fairness and group fairness
Week 10. Fairness: fairness-aware federated learning
Week 11. Ethical and social implications of trustworthy AI
Week 12. Group presentation I
Week 13. Group presentation II
